items.stem: ‘The Great Depression was the main reason for the breakdown of international order in the 1930s.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: It helped bring Hitler to power. It pushed Japan towards expansion in Manchuria. It made Britain and France reluctant to act or rearm. Against: The aims of the dictators, especially Hitler's ideology, drove aggression. Weaknesses of the League existed before the Depression. British and French appeasement was a policy choice. Judgement: the Depression created the conditions for aggression and weakened the will to resist it, but the decisions of the dictators turned crisis into war.

items.stem: ‘The League failed in the 1930s mainly because Britain and France put their own interests first.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: They would not risk war with Japan in the Far East. They wanted Mussolini as an ally and did the Hoare-Laval deal. They feared the economic cost of sanctions during the Depression. Against: The League's structure, unanimity and lack of an army, made action hard. The absence of the USA made sanctions ineffective. The aggressors were determined and simply left the League. Judgement: the League's structural weaknesses mattered, but in each crisis it failed because Britain and France chose not to use the powers it had.

items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: How far was the Abyssinian crisis more damaging to the League than the Manchurian crisis?
items.answer: For: Abyssinia was in Europe's sphere and closer to Britain and France, so failure was more obvious. The Hoare-Laval Pact showed members undermining their own League. It drove Mussolini towards Hitler. Against: Manchuria set the precedent that aggression would go unpunished. Japan's departure showed great powers could defy the League. Both crises revealed the same weaknesses. Judgement: Manchuria showed the League's weakness, but Abyssinia destroyed its credibility because sanctions were imposed and then undermined by its leading members.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (18-20): sustained analysis of both sides of the question, supported by precise evidence, with a well-substantiated judgement. Level 4 (15-17): developed analysis of both sides; a judgement is reached but is not fully supported. Level 3 (10-14): analysis of one side, or of both with limited development or accuracy. Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. Agree / supporting: Abyssinia was in Europe's sphere and closer to Britain and France, so failure was more obvious. The Hoare-Laval Pact showed members undermining their own League. It drove Mussolini towards Hitler. Disagree / other factors: Manchuria set the precedent that aggression would go unpunished. Japan's departure showed great powers could defy the League. Both crises revealed the same weaknesses. Possible judgement: Manchuria showed the League's weakness, but Abyssinia destroyed its credibility because sanctions were imposed and then undermined by its leading members. [20]

items.stem: Study Sources C and D. Source C: a historian writing in 1990 (illustrative). “The League could only be as strong as its members wished it to be, and its structure gave the reluctant every excuse for inaction.” Source D: Haile Selassie, speech to the League Assembly, June 1936 (translated, abridged). “It is collective security: it is the very existence of the League of Nations. It is the confidence that each State is to place in international treaties. God and history will remember your judgment.” Identify one similarity and one difference between Sources C and D on the League's failures in the 1930s.
items.answer: Source C: The historian argues that the League's weakness lay in its members and its structure. Source D: It suggests the League's failure to protect Abyssinia threatened collective security itself. A similarity and a difference must each be supported by details from both sources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a similarity and 1 for supporting it from both sources; 1 mark for a difference and 1 for supporting it from both sources [4]

items.stem: In a revision class, a student says: “The Saar plebiscite of 1935 was held under League supervision.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. About 90 per cent voted to return to Germany.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Explain why Britain followed a policy of appeasement.
items.answer: Fear of another war like 1914-18 and of bombing. Britain was not ready militarily and needed time to rearm. Many felt the Treaty of Versailles was unfair to Germany. The Dominions and the USA would not support war. Communism was seen as a greater threat. Economic problems after the Depression. Judgement: appeasement reflected public fear of war and Britain's military weakness, as well as a genuine belief that German grievances were reasonable.

Level 3 (6-8): explains two or more causes; any judgement is undeveloped. Level 2 (3-5): describes or identifies causes, or explains only one. Level 1 (1-2): general, unsupported points. Indicative content: Fear of another war like 1914-18 and of bombing. Britain was not ready militarily and needed time to rearm. Many felt the Treaty of Versailles was unfair to Germany. The Dominions and the USA would not support war. Communism was seen as a greater threat. Economic problems after the Depression. Possible judgement: appeasement reflected public fear of war and Britain's military weakness, as well as a genuine belief that German grievances were reasonable. [10]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why the occupation of Prague in March 1939 ended appeasement. A: It was the first time Hitler took non-German territory. B: Britain's rearmament had progressed. C: British public opinion turned against further concessions. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: It was the first time Hitler took non-German territory. B: Britain's rearmament had progressed. C: British public opinion turned against further concessions. Possible judgement: Prague proved that Hitler's aims went beyond revising Versailles, which destroyed the case for appeasement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: A student writes: “A. J. P. Taylor argued that Hitler followed a detailed blueprint for war.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. Taylor argued Hitler was an opportunist who exploited the mistakes of others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Jonas is planning an answer to the question: “‘Hitler was responsible for the outbreak of war in 1939.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Jonas could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: others made war more likely, but Hitler's aims and his decision to invade Poland make him primarily responsible. Support: His aims of Lebensraum and overturning Versailles required war. He broke the Munich Agreement by taking Prague. Challenge: Appeasement encouraged him to think Britain would not fight. The Nazi-Soviet Pact made the invasion possible.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why Hitler was prepared to risk war over Poland in 1939. A: German rearmament gave him a temporary advantage. B: He believed Britain and France would back down again. C: He wanted Lebensraum in the east. Which was the most significant? Explain your answer with reference to the other reasons.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: German rearmament gave him a temporary advantage. B: He believed Britain and France would back down again. C: He wanted Lebensraum in the east. Possible judgement: the Nazi-Soviet Pact convinced Hitler that he could attack Poland without a war on two fronts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the US tariff of 1930 that raised duties on imports and provoked retaliation”.
items.answer: Smoot-Hawley Tariff
items.markingKey: Smoot-Hawley Tariff: the US tariff of 1930 that raised duties on imports and provoked retaliation. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: A. J. P. Taylor argued that Hitler followed a detailed blueprint for war.
The League imposed oil sanctions on Italy in 1935.
The Lausanne Conference of 1932 effectively ended reparations.
Britain and France declared war on 1 September 1939.
items.answer: The Lausanne Conference of 1932 effectively ended reparations.
items.markingKey: Germany made no further payments. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Kwame is planning an answer to the question: “‘The Great Depression was the main reason for the breakdown of international order in the 1930s.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Kwame could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the Depression created the conditions for aggression and weakened the will to resist it, but the decisions of the dictators turned crisis into war. Support: It helped bring Hitler to power. It pushed Japan towards expansion in Manchuria. Challenge: The aims of the dictators, especially Hitler's ideology, drove aggression. Weaknesses of the League existed before the Depression.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: How far did the Depression change Japanese foreign policy?
items.answer: For: Collapse of silk exports caused rural poverty. The army gained support for expansion to secure resources. Manchuria was seen as an economic lifeline. Against: Japan had ambitions in China before 1929. The army in Manchuria acted independently. Nationalism and militarism had long roots. Judgement: the Depression greatly strengthened the case for expansion, but it accelerated ambitions that already existed.

Level 2 (6-9): mainly descriptive, with implicit links to the question. Level 1 (1-5): general assertions with little accurate knowledge. items.stem: What is meant by “Manchukuo”?
options: The puppet state set up by Japan in Manchuria in 1932 under the former Chinese emperor Puyi.
The German-speaking free city under League supervision that Hitler demanded in 1939.
The explosion on the South Manchurian Railway in September 1931, staged by Japanese officers.
The strip of land giving Poland access to the sea, which separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany.
items.answer: The puppet state set up by Japan in Manchuria in 1932 under the former Chinese emperor Puyi.
items.markingKey: Manchukuo: the puppet state set up by Japan in Manchuria in 1932 under the former Chinese emperor Puyi. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: Britain and France declared war on 1 September 1939.
Abyssinia was a member of the League of Nations.
A. J. P. Taylor argued that Hitler followed a detailed blueprint for war.
The Smoot-Hawley Tariff reduced US import duties.
items.answer: Abyssinia was a member of the League of Nations.
items.markingKey: It had joined in 1923. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Diego is planning an answer to the question: “‘The League failed in the 1930s mainly because Britain and France put their own interests first.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Diego could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the League's structural weaknesses mattered, but in each crisis it failed because Britain and France chose not to use the powers it had. Support: They would not risk war with Japan in the Far East. They wanted Mussolini as an ally and did the Hoare-Laval deal. Challenge: The League's structure, unanimity and lack of an army, made action hard. The absence of the USA made sanctions ineffective.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a historian writing in 1990 (illustrative). “The League could only be as strong as its members wished it to be, and its structure gave the reluctant every excuse for inaction.” Source B: a memorandum by a British Foreign Office official, 1935 (illustrative). “We cannot risk driving Mussolini into the arms of Hitler. Whatever the League may say, Italy's friendship on the Brenner is worth more to us than Abyssinia.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the League failed in the 1930s mainly because Britain and France put their own interests first?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it stresses structural weakness as well as members' choices. Evaluation: it gives no detailed evidence. Source B supports: it shows British interests overriding collective security. Evaluation: one official's view may not be government policy. Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: Elena is planning an answer to the question: “‘Appeasement was a sensible policy for Britain in the 1930s.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Elena could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: appeasement was understandable given Britain's weakness and public mood, but continuing it after Hitler's aims became clear in 1938 was a serious misjudgement. Support: Britain was not ready for war and used the time to rearm, especially in the air. Public opinion and the Dominions opposed war in 1938. Challenge: It encouraged Hitler to make further demands. It sacrificed Czechoslovakia and its strong defences.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: In a revision class, a student says: “The Nazi-Soviet Pact contained a secret protocol dividing Poland.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. It divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Amara is planning an answer to the question: “How far was the Nazi-Soviet Pact the main cause of the outbreak of war in 1939?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Amara could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the Pact was the immediate trigger that made Hitler confident to attack, but it was a means to his aims rather than the main cause. Support: It removed the threat of a two-front war for Hitler. It made the invasion of Poland possible. Challenge: Hitler's aims were the underlying cause. Appeasement had encouraged him.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Read Source C. Taylor argued that Hitler was a traditional German statesman who exploited opportunities created by others, and that the war of 1939 resulted from diplomatic blunders on all sides. (A. J. P. Taylor, The Origins of the Second World War, 1961 (summary of the argument).) How reliable is Source C as evidence about responsibility for the war? Use the provenance of the source and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Reliable because Taylor was a leading historian who used diplomatic documents. Less reliable because his interpretation was controversial and was criticised for ignoring Nazi ideology. Cross-reference: It does not give weight to Hitler's racial aims. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view, but it needs to be tested against other evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point about the content; up to 2 marks for using the provenance (author, date, purpose, audience) to judge reliability; up to 2 marks for cross-referencing with own knowledge; 1 mark for a supported overall judgement [6]
